parts.article:
Tunnelling under the Thames
 
The first tunnel ever to be built under a major river was the tunnel under London’s River Thames
 
(A) At the beginning of the 19th century, the port of London was the busiest in the world. Cargoes that had travelled thousands of miles and survived all the hazards of the sea were unloaded on the banks of the Thames, only for their owners to discover that the most frustrating portion of their journey lay ahead. Consignments intended for the southern parts of Britain had to be lifted onto horse carts, pulled through the docks and across London Bridge, built in the 12th century and as impractical as its early date implies. By 1820, London Bridge had become the centre of the world’s largest traffic jam.
 
(B) It was an intolerable situation, and it was clear that if private enterprise could build another crossing closer to the docks, there would be good money to be made in tolls paid by users. Another bridge was out of the question, as this would deny sailing ships access to the city centre, and ambitious men turned their thoughts to tunnelling beneath the Thames instead. This was not such an obvious idea as it might appear. Although increasing demand for coal had meant a great many tunnels had been dug in mines in Britain, working methods remained primitive. Tunnels were dug by men with simple tools, by candlelight. However, in 1807, a group of businessmen got themselves up as the Thames Archway Company. Their ambition was to tunnel below the Thames, but there was little to guide them as there had been no previous attempt to do this. Their chief engineer was Richard Trevithick, designer of the world’s first high-pressure steam engine. His men made progress at the beginning, but then things began to go disastrously wrong, with muddy soil pouring into the tunnel. Eventually the Thames Archway Company had had enough. Its funds were exhausted, Trevithick was sick from exposure to the river water, and its efforts had proved only that a passage under the river exceeded the limits of contemporary mining technology.
 
(C) At that time, the only machines used in mines were pumps. It took a man of genius to recognise that a different sort of machine was needed, a machine that could prevent the roof and walls of a tunnel from collapsing. This man was Marc Brunel, a Frenchman who had become one of the most prominent engineers in Britain. Not long after the failure of the Thames Archway Company, Brunel saw a rotten piece of wood lying on the river bank. Examining the wood through a magnifying glass, he observed it was infested with something that looked like a worm. Brunel realised that as it tunnelled through the wood, it would push chewed wood into its mouth and digest it, then excrete a hard substance that lined the new tunnel. Brunel realised that the worm’s digging technique could be adapted to produce a new way of tunnelling. His realisation led him to invent a device that has been used in one form or another in most major tunnels built since: the tunnelling shield. It consisted of a series of iron frames that could be pressed against the tunnel face and supported on a set of horizontal wooden planks that would prevent the face from collapsing. It was a complex machine and not easy to use, but it seemed that it would protect the miners. Brunel’s team examined earth samples taken from beneath the riverbed, and subsequently decided to dig the tunnel close to the muddy river bottom, where he could expect to find clay. This would be a more solid and safe substance to dig through than the sand that was found deeper down.
 
(D) Brunel began work on his tunnel in 1825, but the problems of such an operation soon became apparent. Although the shield itself worked well, water began to drip into the tunnel. This was more of an annoyance than a danger while the pump was working, but this machine proved unreliable and sometimes failed altogether, meaning that floods began to occur with increasing regularity. The miners often had to run for their lives. Even when Brunel’s men were able to work, they complained of frequent headaches, because the air underground was dirty and contaminated due to the lack of an adequate ventilation system. There were other problems too. Illuminating the tunnels was a constant challenge. Lamps gave off only a weak glow, and there were a number of accidents because the miners could not see what they were doing. Lastly, a number of Brunel’s miners walked off the job because they could not tolerate the excessive temperatures that developed in the cramped conditions underground.
 
(E) Despite all the setbacks, the tunnel finally emerged on the opposite river bank on August 12, 1841. Brunel’s triumph, however, was only partial. The small payment of a penny per person made by the thousands of visitors hardly paid the interest on the government loan he had required to complete the project. As a result, there was never enough funding to make it accessible to horse-drawn vehicles, as intended. Instead, the passageways were filled with souvenir-sellers by day and the homeless at night, before it was finally closed.
 
(F) It was only when the underground railway came to London in the 1860s that the Thames Tunnel achieved a measure of real usefulness. It was bought in 1869 by the East London Railway, who found it to be in such excellent condition that it was immediately pressed into service as a route for passenger trains heading east. The tunnel became, and remains, part of the London Underground network.

Q1 In the early 19th century, the port of London was considered a safer destination than other ports.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q2 London Bridge provided quick access for cargo being sent to southern Britain.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q3 It was generally believed that a new river crossing would be profitable.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q4 Building a second bridge crossing was initially considered to be the best solution.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q5 It was believed that coal could be found under the River Thames.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q6 The Thames Archway Company were the first group to try tunnelling below the Thames.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q7 Some of Trevithick’s men were injured during a mudslide at his tunnel.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q8 The Thames Archway Company ran out of money to finance the tunnel project.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

reference:
Q1

解析 原文只说了伦敦港是当时世界上最繁忙的港口，根本没提它是不是比其他港口更“安全（safer）”。

干扰 你可能看到后面提到了货物从海上的危险中幸存下来（survived all the hazards），但这是指海上的情况，并没有把伦敦港和其他港口的安全程度做直接对比。

句子 At the beginning of the 19th century, the port of London was the busiest in the world. Cargoes that had travelled thousands of miles and survived all the hazards of the sea were unloaded on the banks of the Thames, only for their owners to discover that the most frustrating portion of their journey lay ahead.

Q2

解析 原文明确提到通过伦敦桥运输既不切实际（impractical），还造成了世界上最大的交通拥堵（largest traffic jam），这和题目中的“快速通行（quick access）”完全相反。

干扰 你可能看到货物要被运往英国南部（southern parts），就想当然以为有直达通道，但别忽略了“traffic jam（交通拥堵）”这个直接反驳了“快速”的核心词。

句子 Consignments intended for the southern parts of Britain had to be lifted onto horse carts, pulled through the docks and across London Bridge, built in the 12th century and as impractical as its early date implies. By 1820, London Bridge had become the centre of the world’s largest traffic jam.

Q3

解析 原文明确指出，如果建一条新通道，就能通过收过路费赚大钱（good money to be made），这就完美等同于题目里的“有利可图（profitable）”。

干扰 你可能会纠结这是谁的想法，但原文的 it was clear that...（很显然……）正好对应了题目中 generally believed（普遍认为）这种当时的社会共识。

句子 It was an intolerable situation, and it was clear that if private enterprise could build another crossing closer to the docks, there would be good money to be made in tolls paid by users.

Q4

解析 原文明确指出再建一座桥是“根本不可能的（out of the question）”，这和题目里的“最初被认为是最佳方案（best solution）”直接矛盾。

干扰 你可能只看到了 Another bridge（另一座桥），但一定要往后看，后面解释了建桥会阻碍帆船进入市中心，所以人们直接去想挖隧道的事了，建桥根本不是好主意。

句子 Another bridge was out of the question, as this would deny sailing ships access to the city centre, and ambitious men turned their thoughts to tunnelling beneath the Thames instead.

Q5

解析 原文确实提到了人们对煤炭（coal）的需求增加导致英国挖了很多矿道，但压根没提到人们认为“泰晤士河底下有煤炭”。

干扰 你不要看到 coal（煤）和 tunnels（隧道）就激动地选 TRUE，一定要看清楚，煤矿和泰晤士河（River Thames）在原文里是两件没有发生地点重合的事情。

句子 Although increasing demand for coal had meant a great many tunnels had been dug in mines in Britain, working methods remained primitive. Tunnels were dug by men with simple tools, by candlelight. However, in 1807, a group of businessmen got themselves up as the Thames Archway Company. Their ambition was to tunnel below the Thames, but there was little to guide them as there had been no previous attempt to do this.

Q6

解析 原文提到泰晤士隧道公司想在河底挖隧道，并且明确说“以前没有人尝试过（no previous attempt to do this）”，这说明他们就是第一组尝试的人。

干扰 你可能会在原文里死找 first 这个词，但 no previous attempt 就是“他们是第一个吃螃蟹的人”的最强同义替换。

句子 However, in 1807, a group of businessmen got themselves up as the Thames Archway Company. Their ambition was to tunnel below the Thames, but there was little to guide them as there had been no previous attempt to do this.

Q7

解析 原文提到了泥土涌入隧道导致工程出现了灾难性的错误，但完全没有提及任何关于“工人受伤（men were injured）”的信息。

干扰 你可能会凭常识脑补泥石流（muddy soil pouring）一定会导致人员伤亡，但在做判断题时，原文没写就是没写，千万不要自己加戏。

句子 His men made progress at the beginning, but then things began to go disastrously wrong, with muddy soil pouring into the tunnel. Eventually the Thames Archway Company had had enough. Its funds were exhausted, Trevithick was sick from exposure to the river water, and its efforts had proved only that a passage under the river exceeded the limits of contemporary mining technology.

Q8

解析 原文明确说到泰晤士隧道公司的“资金耗尽了（funds were exhausted）”，这就是题目中 ran out of money 的同义替换。

干扰 你可能只注意到了工程师 Trevithick 生病了，但是要看全整个并列句，funds were exhausted 就是最直接的没钱了的证据。

句子 Eventually the Thames Archway Company had had enough. Its funds were exhausted, Trevithick was sick from exposure to the river water, and its efforts had proved only that a passage under the river exceeded the limits of contemporary mining technology.

Q9

解析 原文说 Brunel 观察到木头里有一种看起来像“虫子（worm）”的东西，并在后面详细描述了这虫子是如何在木头里钻洞（tunnelled through the wood）的，完美对应题目。

干扰 你可能会想填 something，但是 looked like a worm 明确给出了这种生物的具象名称，且只有 worm 符合生物打洞的语境。

句子 Examining the wood through a magnifying glass, he observed it was infested with something that looked like a worm. Brunel realised that as it tunnelled through the wood, it would push chewed wood into its mouth and digest it, then excrete a hard substance that lined the new tunnel. Brunel realised that the worm’s digging technique could be adapted to produce a new way of tunnelling.

Q10

解析 原文提到 Brunel 决定把隧道挖在靠近泥泞河底的地方（即浅层 shallow tunnel），因为他希望在那里能找到“黏土（clay）”。

干扰 你可能会被后一句的 sand（沙子）干扰，但原文说 sand 是在更深的地方（deeper down），而题目问的是 shallow tunnel 里的成分，所以只能是 clay。

句子 Brunel’s team examined earth samples taken from beneath the riverbed, and subsequently decided to dig the tunnel close to the muddy river bottom, where he could expect to find clay. This would be a more solid and safe substance to dig through than the sand that was found deeper down.

Q11

解析 原文直接写道矿工们抱怨经常患“头痛（headaches）”，原因正是地下空气肮脏受污染。

干扰 你可能会在原文死找 pollution 这个词，但原文用了 dirty and contaminated 做同义替换，顺着这个原因往前看很容易找到对应的病症 headaches。

句子 Even when Brunel’s men were able to work, they complained of frequent headaches, because the air underground was dirty and contaminated due to the lack of an adequate ventilation system.

Q12

解析 原文提到灯光微弱导致矿工看不清（即 lighting problems），因此引发了许多“事故（accidents）”。

干扰 你可能看到了 weak glow 就想填 glow，但题目问的是照明问题导致了什么“后果（led to several...）”，所以必须往后看到 a number of accidents。

句子 Illuminating the tunnels was a constant challenge. Lamps gave off only a weak glow, and there were a number of accidents because the miners could not see what they were doing.

Q13

解析 原文说明游客付的那点微薄门票钱，连支付“政府（government）”贷款的利息都不够，对应了题目中需要偿还债务的对象。

干扰 你可能会想填 loan（贷款）或者 interest（利息），但题目问的是“repay his debt to the...（把债还给谁）”，这里的债主是 government，且题目限制 ONE WORD ONLY，所以只能填 government。

句子 The small payment of a penny per person made by the thousands of visitors hardly paid the interest on the government loan he had required to complete the project. As a result, there was never enough funding to make it accessible to horse-drawn vehicles, as intended.
